falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant differences in surface phase composition, oxidation state, and subsequent phase evolution (or mechanical properties) are found between samples processed in inert versus mildly oxidizing atmospheres, then the role of Al surface oxidation in controlling phase stability is not supported.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s indication that Al oxidation during plasma spraying can locally deplete Al and alter phase stability
hypotheses.what_is_new: It extends this observation to a Cr-rich Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy and tests whether even minimal Al oxidation can act as a trigger for localized changes in phase stability upon thermal exposure.

paper_did: Synthesized FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 ingots by induction melting in an argon atmosphere, followed by casting, melting for homogenization, and subsequent gas atomization to produce spherical powder with a narrow size distribution.

Consolidated the powder into bulk samples via laser powder bed fusion (L‐PBF) and as coatings using microplasma spraying (MPS), and then applied post‐processing heat treatments (annealing at 600 °C and 900 °C for 1 hour in air).

Characterized the materials extensively using XRD, SEM, EDS, DTA, microhardness testing, and nanoindentation to analyze phase composition, microstructure, element segregation, and mechanical properties.
paper_reported: Gas atomization produced a dendritic, supersaturated BCC solid solution with slight Mo‐rich and Al‐rich segregations, while L‐PBF samples maintained a similar microstructure with more pronounced liquation of heavy elements.
The MPS coatings exhibited inhomogeneity due to Al oxidation during spraying, which created Al-depleted regions that stabilized a minor FCC phase alongside the BCC.

Annealing at 600 °C increased microhardness (~950 HV) via enhanced elemental segregation and elastic stress development, and annealing at 900 °C resulted in decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution into B2 and σ phases with a moderate hardness reduction.
paper_proposed: Investigating the evolution of non-equilibrium microstructures under different consolidation methods and annealing conditions to better control phase stability and mechanical properties.
Addressing challenges associated with the inhomogeneity and oxidation effects in plasma-sprayed coatings, as high-temperature annealing led to property deterioration.

paper_did: Produced a gas‐atomized FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high‐entropy alloy powder from high‐purity elemental ingots using rapid melt solidification and a gas atomization process.
Conducted a systematic series of annealing experiments between 300 °C and 800 °C for various times (1, 3, 9, and 27 h) in an air atmosphere.

Characterized phase evolution and microstructural changes using X‐ray diffraction (noting BCC/B2 phases, lattice parameter shifts, and the emergence of sigma phase), scanning electron microscopy with EDS (revealing elemental segregation and nanoscale modulations), and measured microhardness to relate elastic misfit to strengthening.

Estimated activation energies for the early stage of decomposition (~0.65 eV, attributed to quenched vacancy‐assisted Al diffusion) and for sigma phase formation (~2.6 eV, comparable to self‐diffusion in BCC metals).
paper_reported: Annealing in the range 300–600 °C increases elemental segregation causing an increase in lattice misfit up to 1.5% and a corresponding rise in microhardness (up to ~1070 HV) that follows a linear relation (dHV/dε = 43400 MPa).
Sigma phase nucleation occurs when the maximum elastic deformation is reached (ε = 1.5 %), typically forming at the semi‐coherent boundaries, thereby further modifying the microhardness response.

A very low activation energy (0.65 eV) for the initial stage of solid solution decomposition was observed, suggesting that quenched vacancies facilitate Al atom migration and thus rapid early spinodal decomposition.
The paper discussed the role of nanoscale compositional modulations (spinodal decomposition) and elastic stress from element partitioning as key mechanisms for the observed strengthening.
paper_proposed: That post‐manufacturing heat treatments in the 400–500 °C range (where diffusion is active but sigma phase formation can be avoided) can be used to tailor internal stress and strengthening in additive manufacturing and thermal spray applications.
Avoiding sigma phase formation (which starts above ~600 °C) is crucial as its emergence leads to additional internal stresses and can detract from the desired mechanical properties.

The kinetics of this ordering transformation depend strongly on the cooling history.

paper_did: Fabricated an equimolar Ti–V–Nb–Ta refractory high‐entropy alloy using high‐purity elements, followed by vacuum melting and a 7‑day homogenization at 1200°C.
Subjected the homogenized alloy to thermal aging at 700°C for different durations (1, 5, and 40 days) to study long‐term stability.

Employed a range of advanced microstructural characterization techniques (SEM, EDX, EBSD, TKD, STEM, 3D FIB/SEM, and APT) and nanoindentation to assess the evolution of phases and mechanical properties.
Performed CALPHAD calculations to model phase stability and demonstrated that even trace oxygen (and nitrogen) can trigger the formation of an α‑Ti phase.

Observed that aging induces the nucleation of Ti‑enriched precipitates (both at grain boundaries and intragranularly) along with the formation of precipitate‐free zones (PFZs), leading to age softening (hardness decrease from ~5.05 GPa to ~4.22 GPa).
paper_reported: The homogenized Ti–V–Nb–Ta alloy exhibits a single‐phase, homogeneous BCC structure.

Thermal aging at 700°C causes the precipitation of Ti‑enriched α‑Ti phase (with HCP structure) via the Burgers orientation relationship, which nucleates first at grain boundaries and later within grains.

Trace interstitial impurities (oxygen and nitrogen) initially contribute to solid solution strengthening but, upon partitioning into precipitates, deplete the matrix of interstitials and reduce lattice distortions, resulting in age softening.
Quantitative analysis indicates that the precipitate volume fraction (around 3%) contributes minimally to hardness compared to the loss of interstitial strengthening.
CALPHAD modeling confirms that even small amounts of oxygen stabilize the α‑Ti phase at 700°C.
paper_proposed: Improving impurity control (especially oxygen and nitrogen) during processing to maintain microstructural and mechanical stability at high temperatures.
Exploring the balance between precipitate hardening and reduced solid solution strengthening due to interstitial depletion, with an eye toward enhancing alloy performance over long service lifetimes.
Incorporating impurity‐driven effects into the design and scaling‐up of RHEAs for high‑temperature structural applications, such as those in nuclear reactors.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by diffusion‐limited ordering kinetics: slower cooling permits sufficient atomic mobility for chemical short‐range ordering and segregation (especially of Cr and Al), leading to phase separation from the high-temperature BCC state, whereas rapid quenching retains the metastable BCC phase.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature BCC state.
hypotheses.intervention: Vary the cooling rate from the high-temperature state using controlled rapid quenching versus slow cooling.
hypotheses.conditions: Cooling rates that allow significant atomic diffusion (slow cooling) versus rates that freeze atomic positions (rapid quench); experiments can be performed under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Development of chemical short-range order (SRO) and microsegregation patterns.
hypotheses.mechanism: During slow cooling, atoms (particularly Cr and Al) have time to diffuse, promoting ordering and local compositional fluctuations that trigger phase separation (e.g., formation of secondary precipitates), while rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and retains the single-phase BCC structure. This resembles how SRO and ODTT influence phase stability in refractory HEAs (PMC10154406::web::012 and PMC10154406::web::013).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled samples will exhibit formation of secondary phases or precipitates (detectable by XRD/TEM/APT), and corresponding microstructural inhomogeneities, whereas quenched samples remain predominantly single-phase BCC.
hypotheses.baseline: A rapidly quenched sample that minimizes diffusion and ordering.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism should apply in cooling regimes that permit atomic mobility; if the cooling is extremely rapid, ordering is kinetically frozen and no additional phases appear.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise temperature window and diffusion kinetics for Cr and Al in this multi-component alloy are not fully known, hence the exact scale of phase fraction change is uncertain.

hypotheses.builds_on: The finding that SRO and order–disorder transitions (ODTT) crucially affect phase stability in refractory HEAs (PMC10154406) and related materials.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It applies the principle of diffusion-controlled ordering and segregation to explain phase evolution in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 during cooling, a condition not previously explored in the paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Minor doping with titanium (Ti) stabilizes the BCC phase by lowering the effective valence electron concentration (VEC), thereby shifting the order–disorder transition temperature and reducing the driving force for phase separation during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature BCC state.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a small amount (approximately 1–2 at%) of Ti into the alloy composition.
hypotheses.conditions: Experiments should be conducted using the same cooling and thermal exposure conditions for doped and undoped samples, ensuring that Ti is uniformly distributed without forming its own intermetallics; performed under inert or controlled atmospheres.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Modification of electronic concentration and local bonding environment that alters the SRO evolution and delays the onset of ordering-induced phase separation.
hypotheses.mechanism: Ti, being a Group IV element, reduces the overall VEC—similar to how Hf was used in the referenced study (PMC10154406::web::007)—which shifts the ODTT downward. This postpones or suppresses the formation of detrimental chemical clusters. Consequently, the doped alloy will retain its single-phase BCC structure over a broader temperature range compared to the undoped counterpart.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Ti-doped Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will show improved phase stability, with fewer or no secondary precipitates, as evidenced by consistent BCC diffraction patterns and homogenous microstructures after cooling and moderate thermal exposures, relative to the undoped alloy.
hypotheses.baseline: Undoped Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 processed under identical conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: This effect should be observed only when Ti doping remains low (around 1–2 at%); excessive Ti could introduce new intermetallic phases or change other properties adversely.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the anticipated direction of the effect is supported by VEC principles, the precise amount of doping required and its influence on the kinetics of ordering in this specific alloy need validation.

hypotheses.builds_on: The mechanism of VEC lowering used in designing refractory HEAs (as shown in PMC10154406) and the known impact of Group IV elements on phase stability.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces a microalloying approach using Ti into Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 to manipulate the electronic structure and modify phase stability, a parameter not investigated in the original paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Reversible phase transitions in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 are induced by operating near its order–disorder transition temperature (ODTT); thermal cycling through this critical region triggers reversible changes in short-range order (SRO), leading to periodic appearance or disappearance of secondary phases.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature BCC state.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject the alloy to cyclic thermal annealing treatments that approach and recede from the expected ODTT region, using controlled dwell times at temperatures near the predicted ODTT.
hypotheses.conditions: Thermal cycles should be performed in a controlled inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with temperature ramps that approach the ODTT from below and above; baseline comparisons should include samples held at temperatures well outside the ODTT region.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Reversible modulation of SRO that governs the stability of the BCC phase versus the emergence of secondary phases.
hypotheses.mechanism: When heated near the ODTT, the balance between entropy and enthalpy shifts, causing reversible changes in the degree of atomic ordering. This alters local chemical environments, potentially inducing transient phase separation or homogenization. Upon cooling, these changes are reversed. This mechanism is analogous to the modeled SRO transitions in the refractory HEA system (PMC10154406::web::010), but applied to CrCoFeNiAl to explain temperature-dependent phase appearance.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples undergoing thermal cycling near the ODTT will show reversible signatures in phase composition: secondary phase diffraction peaks (or corresponding microstructural features) will appear when the sample is held near the ODTT and disappear when cycled away, while samples processed entirely outside this critical region will show irreversible phase states.
hypotheses.baseline: Samples annealed at temperatures far below or well above the ODTT, where the phase structure remains stable.
hypotheses.boundary: This phenomenon should be observable only when annealing temperatures are within a narrow window close to the ODTT; outside this window, phase changes should not be reversible.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact ODTT for Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is not precisely known, and the magnitude of reversible phase changes may be subtle and require sensitive characterization.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no reversible phase or SRO changes are detected upon cycling near the ODTT, or if the phase structure remains unchanged regardless of thermal history, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: Insights from modeling of order–disorder transitions and SRO effects in refractory HEAs (PMC10154406::web::010) as well as general principles of reversible phase behavior in alloy systems.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a thermal cycling protocol to directly test the reversibility of SRO-driven phase changes in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, a mechanism not explored in the paper, to account for the observed diversity in phase behavior.

paper_did: Designed and synthesized quinary refractory HEA films (W‐Ta‐Cr‐V‐Hf) via magnetron sputtering (thin ~100 nm and thick ~3 µm films) based on thermophysical calculations, CALPHAD, and cluster expansion methods.

Carried out in situ TEM annealing at 1173 K and various ion irradiation experiments (16 keV He implantation; dual‐beam irradiation with 1 MeV Kr+ + 16 keV He+), as well as ex situ Ar irradiation for hardness measurements.

Characterized grain size evolution (grain growth under He implantation and grain refinement under dual‐beam irradiation), defect formation (no dislocation loops but formation and saturation of cavities), and compositional evolution (via EDX and APT showing Hf segregation and later homogenization).

Performed nanoindentation hardness tests showing progressive hardening after annealing and irradiation, and provided mechanistic insights based on SRO transitions, ballistic mixing, and defect recombination via high grain-boundary density.
paper_reported: High thermal stability of the quinary RHEA with minimal grain coarsening and, under dual-beam irradiation, grain refinement attributed to cascade fragmentation events.

Excellent irradiation resistance evidenced by an absence of dislocation loop formation even up to 8.5 dpa and high He implantation levels, along with uniformly distributed but saturating cavity formation.

Increased hardness after thermal and irradiation exposures, with APT analyses demonstrating a change from compositional striations (with layered Cr-V-Hf versus W-Ta regions) in the as-deposited state to a homogeneous elemental distribution post-irradiation.

An underpinning mechanism that leverages chemical complexity, controlled SRO, and design strategies (via VEC and ODTT tuning) to suppress undesirable phase separation or precipitation under extreme conditions.
paper_proposed: The methodology combining computational thermodynamics (including CALPHAD and cluster expansion) with experimental validation is proposed as a design route to rapidly assess and develop new HEA/RHEA systems for reactor-relevant extreme environments.

Future work was suggested in exploring compositional modifications to tailor irradiation resistance and thermal stability (e.g., mitigating precipitation issues observed in previous quaternary alloys) for applications over different temperature regimes.

hypotheses.boundary: The mechanism should apply if the isothermal hold temperature is maintained just below the order–disorder transition temperature. Elemental analyses demonstrated temperature‐sensitive segregation phenomena (e.g., Hf segregation upon annealing and subsequent homogenization under irradiation) that correlate with computed SRO parameters and ODTT.

Nanoindentation results showed a significant increase in hardness (from 13.25 GPa unirradiated to 20 GPa after irradiation) attributable to factors including defect density, lattice distortion, and grain size refinement.

paper_did: Processed a single‐phase, body‐centered cubic HfNbTiZr multi‐principal element alloy using high‐pressure torsion (HPT) with varying numbers of turns (½, 1, 5, and 10) to impose a wide range of shear strains (from ~3 to ~340).

Subjected the SPD‐processed disks to rapid thermal treatments – annealing at 740, 890, and 1000 K – using controlled heating (40 K/min) and quenching (300 K/min), and sampled from both the disk center and edge.

Characterized the microstructure and phase composition via X‐ray diffraction (with Lorentzian peak fitting), X‐ray line profile analysis (XLPA), electron microscopy (SEM, TEM, EBSD), and hardness testing to monitor grain size, dislocation density, phase decomposition, and anneal‐induced hardening.
paper_reported: That annealing the nanocrystalline HfNbTiZr alloy (after SPD) induces decomposition of the initial single bcc phase into two distinct bcc variants (bccL and bccH) at 740 K, with further formation of an hcp phase at higher temperatures (notably above 890 K).

A strong correlation between the imposed shear strain (from the SPD treatment) and the details of phase decomposition, including changes in lattice parameters, phase fractions, and chemical heterogeneities, was observed.

Observed grain refinement (with crystallite sizes saturating around 15 nm) and a significant reduction in dislocation density upon annealing in the bccH phase, which together influence the hardness evolution of the alloy.
paper_proposed: An extension of previous single‐location studies to systematically examine the influence of spatially varying shear strains (center vs. edge of the disks) on thermal stability.
Further correlation between microstructural changes (phase composition, grain refinement, and recovery) and mechanical properties (hardness) in the context of high‐temperature applications.
Implicitly, a future avenue for research into optimizing annealing treatments and understanding heterogeneous elemental segregation in SPD‐processed multi‐principal element alloys.

paper_did: Synthesized a homogeneous high‐temperature Hf25Nb25Ti25Zr25 multi‐principal element alloy (MPEA) via magnetic levitation melting followed by homogenization at 1290 °C.

Processed the alloy into 0.85‐mm‐thick disks and applied severe plastic deformation (SPD) using high‐pressure torsion (HPT) at various numbers of turns (½, 1, 5, and 10) to create a wide range of shear strains (from ~3 up to ~340) at different locations (center vs. edge).
Subjected the HPT‐processed specimens to annealing treatments at 740 K, 890 K, and 1000 K (with controlled heating/quenching rates) to study thermal responses.

Characterized the phase composition, crystallite size, dislocation density, and microstructural evolution using X‐ray diffraction (including X-ray line-profile analysis), electron microscopy (EBSD, TEM, EDS), and hardness measurements.
paper_reported: Observed that SPD refines the microstructure – reducing crystallite size (down to ~15 nm) and building up high dislocation densities (up to ~220×10^14 m^−2) – with these parameters saturating above a shear strain of ~30.

Found that annealing at 740 K leads to the decomposition of the original BCC phase into two distinct BCC phases (denoted as bccL with a higher lattice parameter and bccH with a lower lattice parameter), which are attributed to elemental segregation (with larger elements Hf/Zr favoring bccL and smaller Nb/Ti favoring bccH).

Reported that at higher temperatures (890 K and 1000 K) an additional hcp phase can form (especially in high‐strain regions) and that anneal-induced hardening occurs under certain conditions, while also noting recovery (e.g., a decrease in dislocation density and increase in crystallite size) in the bccH phase during annealing.
paper_proposed: Extended previous work by exploring how different levels of SPD (assessed via HPT turns and sampling from the disk center versus edge) affect phase stability and decomposition during annealing in a HfNbTiZr MPEA.

Implied that further research could correlate the spatial heterogeneities (in phase fractions and chemical composition) with local deformation parameters, although no explicit new mechanistic intervention (e.g., defect‐specific studies) was proposed.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Phase stability is governed by a cooling-rate–dependent spinodal decomposition induced by subtle compositional fluctuations in the BCC matrix that are amplified by differential elemental diffusivities.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature BCC state, assumed to be compositionally homogeneous at high temperature.
hypotheses.intervention: Perform two cooling protocols: a rapid quench versus a controlled slow cooling, and include an isothermal hold (e.g., 750–800 °C) during slow cooling to promote diffusion.
hypotheses.conditions: This mechanism should be active during cooling from the high-temperature BCC phase in conditions where diffusion is not completely frozen out (i.e., moderate to slow cooling). It should not apply if the cooling is too rapid to allow any significant diffusion or if the temperature never enters the metastable regime (below about 800 °C).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A modulation in local composition results in the development of a lamellar or interconnected pattern of new phases within the BCC matrix.
hypotheses.mechanism: Differential diffusivities of the constituent elements (especially Al and transition metals with different atomic sizes) lead to local concentration fluctuations when cooling is slow. These fluctuations cross the spinodal limit, triggering a spontaneous decomposition into compositionally modulated regions that act as precursors for the nucleation of intermetallic phases. This is similar in spirit to the spinodal decomposition phenomena discussed in the paper where metastable phase formation was attributed to compositional modulation (e.g., PMC7956699::web::014, PMC7956699::web::015) and is supported by general concepts of spinodal decomposition from background materials.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Controlled slow cooling (with or without an isothermal hold) will lead to a characteristic, fine-scale, lamellar or interconnected secondary phase pattern observable via microscopy (e.g., SEM/EDS and EBSD) in contrast to a relatively homogeneous, metastable BCC phase in the quenched sample. The difference is expected to be significant (i.e., clear microstructural evolution) though precise quantitative phase fractions may be uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Rapid quenching from the high-temperature BCC state, which should retain a largely homogeneous phase without significant compositional modulation.
hypotheses.boundary: The hypothesis applies when the temperature window allows atomic mobility (e.g., between roughly 750 °C and 800 °C) and when the cooling rate is not so fast that diffusion is negligible. It should not apply under conditions where cooling is instantaneous or under prolonged exposures at temperatures well below the diffusion activation range.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact temperature range for the onset of spinodal decomposition in this alloy is not precisely known, and the quantitative extent of phase modulation is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in microstructure or phase formation is detected between the quenched and slow-cooled samples, or if both conditions yield a homogeneous BCC phase without evidence of spinodal decomposition, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation of exothermic phase transformations and compositional modulations at around 800 °C (PMC7956699::web::009, PMC7956699::web::014) suggests a role for diffusion-driven instabilities. This hypothesis extends that reasoning to explain phase stability in a related but Al-containing alloy.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes that the range of phases in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 originates primarily from cooling-rate–controlled spinodal decomposition, a factor not previously isolated, and recommends a controlled cooling experiment to distinguish the diffusion-driven mechanism.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Interfacial lattice strain, arising from mismatches between the primary BCC matrix and early-stage coherent precipitates, governs the transformation pathway and phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature, single-phase BCC state.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a controlled modification of the interfacial energy by pre-introducing a fine dispersion of inert nanoparticles (or oxide dispersoids) that interact with forming precipitates during controlled cooling.
hypotheses.conditions: This mechanism should be effective when the alloy is cooled slowly enough for coherent precipitates to form and for interfacial strain energy to become a dominant factor. It is not expected to operate if no such interacting interface modifiers are added or if the cooling rate is so high as to preclude coherent interface development.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent or semi-coherent precipitates (such as early intermetallic forms) at the interfaces within the BCC matrix.
hypotheses.mechanism: During cooling, elemental partitioning leads to the nucleation of coherent intermetallic precipitates; however, the lattice mismatch between these nascent phases and the BCC matrix produces localized strain fields. These strain fields lower the barrier for further transformation and dictate which phase variants become stabilized. By altering the effective interfacial energy (through the addition of inert dispersoids that interact with these regions), one can modulate the nucleation kinetics and growth morphology of the secondary phases. This mechanism is conceptually analogous to the role of lattice strains in maraging steels (TXT::wikipedia::Maraging_steel::004) and interfaces in HEAs (KG::interface::1455498deb).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples with the interfacial modifier will show a shift in the transformation sequence, evidenced by either an increased fraction of a specific intermetallic phase (e.g., a coherent ordered phase) or altered precipitate morphology, compared to unmodified samples. The change should be appreciable in terms of precipitate size and distribution.
hypotheses.baseline: Samples processed under identical cooling conditions without the addition of any interfacial modifiers.
hypotheses.boundary: The hypothesis applies under processing conditions where coherent precipitate formation is kinetically accessible (moderate cooling rates, temperature window conducive to atomic ordering). It would not be valid if additional phases nucleate independently of interfacial strain effects (e.g., under extremely slow cooling with near-complete homogenization).
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimal concentration and type of interfacial modifier and the quantitative impact of lattice strain on transformation kinetics require further calibration.

hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces the concept of intentionally modifying interfacial characteristics (via dispersoids) to test whether lattice mismatch strain is the key factor governing phase evolution in this alloy, a variable not previously isolated in related studies.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Aluminum-induced ordering triggers a metastable intermediate phase formation that governs subsequent phase stability during thermal exposure; the ordering kinetics and resulting precipitate morphology depend on the thermal hold time at intermediate temperatures.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 starting in a high-temperature BCC state, with Al uniformly distributed.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a controlled aging treatment at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 600–700 °C) for varying durations after initial cooling to encourage Al-driven ordering.
hypotheses.conditions: This mechanism is expected to operate under conditions where the thermal energy is sufficient to allow atomic shuffling and ordering (aging temperatures around 600–700 °C) but not so high as to revert the alloy to the high-temperature disordered BCC state. It should not apply if the alloy is rapidly quenched to room temperature without any holding or if the temperature exceeds the ordering window.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered intermetallic precipitates (possibly B2-type or other Al-rich phases) within the disordered BCC matrix.
hypotheses.mechanism: Aluminum, being both a strong ordering element and a contributor to lattice distortion, facilitates short-range order during aging. As the alloy is held at an intermediate temperature, localized ordering occurs, leading to the nucleation of metastable intermetallic phases which may serve as precursors to further transformation. The degree of ordering (and hence the subsequent phase stability) depends on the aging time; longer holds lead to coarsening and possible transformation into equilibrium phases. This mechanism draws on principles similar to those underlying precipitation hardening in maraging steels (TXT::wikipedia::Maraging_steel::004) and on observations of ordering phenomena in HEAs (PMC7956699::web::017).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Aging treatments at 600–700 °C will produce a discernible ordered phase (detectable by distinct diffraction peaks via XRD or by distinct crystallography in EBSD), with the volume fraction and coarseness of the phase increasing with aging time compared to a baseline of no aging. The effect should be measurable as a shift in mechanical properties (e.g., increased hardness due to precipitate strengthening).
hypotheses.baseline: Samples that are rapidly cooled to room temperature without any intermediate aging hold, which should primarily retain the metastable BCC structure with minimal ordering.
hypotheses.boundary: The hypothesis applies within a defined aging temperature window (approximately 600–700 °C) and hold times that are long enough to allow ordering but short enough to avoid complete transition to the equilibrium state. It would not hold outside this temperature range or if the alloy composition does not support significant Al-driven ordering.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise nature and crystal structure of the potential ordered phase (e.g., whether it is B2 or another intermetallic form) and the quantitative kinetics of ordering are not well-established.

Analyze phases by XRD and EBSD, and test hardness.

Hardness testing to correlate microstructural changes with mechanical properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If aging treatments do not result in any evidence of ordering (no new diffraction peaks or ordered domains) or if mechanical properties remain unchanged relative to the baseline sample without aging, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The metastable behavior observed in the paper is linked to compositional modulations and intermetallic formation (PMC7956699::web::010, PMC7956699::web::017). This hypothesis leverages the known ordering propensity of Al (as seen in similar high-strength alloys) to propose that Al-driven ordering is a critical factor in phase stability.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It specifically isolates the role of Al-induced ordering in governing the transformation from a disordered BCC state to an ordered metastable intermetallic state and proposes a systematic aging study to test the kinetics and stability of the resulting phases.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Grain Boundary Segregation Drives Local Phase Transformations.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy in the high-temperature BCC (A2) state.
hypotheses.intervention: Control cooling rate and post-cooling grain size by preparing samples with fast quenching versus controlled slow cooling, which alters the density and character of grain boundaries.
hypotheses.conditions: Applies during thermal exposure when sufficient diffusion can occur (≥600 °C) and in alloys containing beta stabilizers; should not apply if the grain boundary area is minimized (e.g., in ultrafine-grained samples produced by severe plastic deformation where boundaries are uniformly saturated).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries acting as preferred sites for solute segregation.
hypotheses.mechanism: During cooling from the high-temperature BCC state, differential segregation of solutes (e.g., Co, Al) to grain boundaries alters local compositions. This localized enrichment/depletion lowers the local transformation barrier and promotes nucleation of secondary phases (such as intermetallic or ordered phases) along boundaries. The paper shows that grain boundary wetting by A2 phase at high annealing temperatures modifies phase composition (see PMC9958938::web::017::4_discussion), suggesting that boundary phenomena strongly influence phase stability. By extrapolating this to CrCoFeNiAl, the hypothesis posits that increased grain boundary segregation during slow cooling induces a split in phase stability.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Slowly cooled samples with more pronounced and chemically enriched grain boundary regions will show an increased fraction of secondary, lower-temperature equilibrium phases and observable grain boundary wetting phenomena relative to rapidly quenched samples.
hypotheses.baseline: Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 that retains a homogeneous high-temperature BCC phase with minimal segregation.
hypotheses.boundary: If the cooling rate is so fast that grain boundary segregation does not develop, then the secondary phases will be suppressed; similarly, if the alloy is processed by severe plastic deformation that alters segregation dynamics, the mechanism might not apply.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of segregation and its precise influence on phase fraction are experimentally uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples: one quenched rapidly from the BCC stability regime and another slowly cooled to allow grain growth and boundary segregation. Characterize the microstructure using high-resolution SEM and XRD.
measurements: Grain boundary composition via EDS or atom probe tomography
Phase fraction determinations via XRD and transmission electron microscopy
Observation of grain boundary wetting layers if present
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both samples show the same phase composition and no significant enrichment at grain boundaries, the hypothesis that segregation drives the phase transformation would be refuted.

hypotheses.builds_on: The evidence in the paper regarding grain boundary wetting (PMC9958938::web::017::4_discussion) and segregation effects during severe plastic deformation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis translates the boundary wetting and segregation mechanisms observed in the TiZrHfMoCrCo alloy to a CrCoFeNiAl system, explicitly proposing a controlled cooling experiment to diagnose the role of grain boundary segregation in phase stability.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Vacancy-Enhanced Diffusion Triggers Secondary Phase Nucleation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy homogenized in its high-temperature BCC state.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a pre-aging anneal at a moderate temperature designed to reduce excess vacancies in one set of samples versus no pre-anneal treatment in a control set.
hypotheses.conditions: Applies during subsequent thermal exposure where vacancy-mediated diffusion is significant (typically 600–1000 °C). Does not apply if the alloy’s vacancy concentration is intrinsically low (e.g., after long high-temperature holding) or if diffusion barriers are intentionally introduced.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Vacancy concentration within the BCC matrix.
hypotheses.mechanism: During cooling from the high-temperature state, a high concentration of vacancies may be retained. These vacancies enhance atomic mobility and enable local reordering (or solute clustering) that favors the nucleation of secondary phases. The paper discusses that HPT can simulate an ‘effective’ high temperature via defect accumulation (PMC9958938::web::016::4_discussion). In the CrCoFeNiAl system, vacancies could similarly drive non-homogeneous diffusion, causing local chemical fluctuations that lower the barrier for transformation away from the BCC phase.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples undergoing a pre-anneal that reduces vacancies prior to aging will have a lower fraction of secondary phases compared to those that retain high vacancy levels. The measurable differences should manifest in phase fraction and lattice parameter changes observed by XRD.
hypotheses.baseline: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 processed directly from the high-temperature BCC state with rapid cooling, retaining a high vacancy concentration.
hypotheses.boundary: The effect is expected only under conditions where vacancy mobility is active (above room temperature, typically in the 600–1000 °C range); if the subsequent thermal exposure is too short or below diffusion thresholds, the mechanism may not operate.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact vacancy concentration and its spatial distribution are hard to measure directly, and their quantitative impact on phase nucleation remains moderately uncertain.

Subject both sets to identical further thermal exposure. Characterize vacancy recovery (via positron annihilation spectroscopy) and phase composition (via XRD and TEM).
measurements: Vacancy concentration measurements
Phase fraction analysis

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pre-annealed (vacancy-reduced) samples show the same extent of secondary phase formation as the control samples, then the hypothesis that vacancies are driving the phase transformation is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The defect accumulation and effective temperature concept discussed in the paper (PMC9958938::web::016::4_discussion) and known vacancy-driven diffusion theories.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies the idea of defect (vacancy) enhanced diffusion—a mechanism noted in severe plastic deformation regimes—to rationalize the observed phase transformations in a CrCoFeNiAl alloy, proposing a concrete pre-anneal treatment to test the role of vacancies.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Kinetically Limited Diffusion Leads to Spatially Heterogeneous Phase Transformation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy initially in a homogeneous high-temperature BCC phase.
hypotheses.intervention: Systematically vary the cooling rate from the high-temperature state (e.g., extremely rapid quenching versus slow furnace cooling) to control the extent of diffusion-driven phase transformation.
hypotheses.conditions: This hypothesis applies when cooling rates are within a range where atomic mobility is neither completely arrested (ultrafast quench) nor fully equilibrated (prolonged isothermal hold). It may not apply if the alloy is annealed long enough at low temperature to reach complete equilibrium.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Local differences in solute distribution and diffusional barriers created by kinetic limitations.
hypotheses.mechanism: Due to the sluggish diffusion typical of high-entropy alloys, the cooling rate strongly influences whether the alloy can locally adjust composition to nucleate the equilibrium secondary phase(s). In regions where cooling is slower (or local microstructural features, like thicker grain regions, permit enhanced diffusion), the BCC phase will transform into secondary phases, while rapidly cooled regions will retain the metastable BCC structure. The paper’s discussion on phase transformation limits and how annealing temperature alters phase fractions (PMC9958938::web::007 to PMC9958938::web::009) supports the idea that kinetics can dictate the equilibrium phase state.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled samples will display a bimodal microstructure with significant fractions of secondary phases (e.g., intermetallic or ordered variants) alongside residual BCC, while rapidly quenched samples will predominantly remain in the BCC phase. XRD patterns and microstructural imaging should reveal correlated differences in phase composition.
hypotheses.baseline: A sample cooled extremely rapidly from the high-temperature BCC state, expected to largely retain that phase due to diffusion limitations.
hypotheses.boundary: If the cooling rate is below a kinetic threshold (i.e., extended hold times), then complete equilibrium is reached, so the observed heterogeneity vanishes; similarly, ultrafast cooling may suppress all transformations, rendering the hypothesis inapplicable.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise time scales and temperature windows relevant to diffusion in this multi-principal element alloy are not well established and must be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture a series of samples subjected to a range of controlled cooling rates from the high-temperature BCC state. Use XRD, TEM, and atom probe analysis to quantify the phase fractions and local compositions.
measurements: Cooling rate control and recording

Local composition mapping via atom probe or TEM-EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no systematic variation in phase fractions or microstructural heterogeneity correlated with the cooling rate, then the hypothesis that kinetically limited diffusion causes heterogeneous phase transformations is refuted.

hypotheses.builds_on: The discussion in the paper regarding how different annealing temperatures and exposure times modify phase composition (PMC9958938::web::009 and PMC9958938::web::010::4_discussion) and classic diffusion‐controlled phase transformation principles.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically addresses the role of cooling rate as a kinetic control parameter in CrCoFeNiAl alloys, proposing a detailed parametric study to map the diffusion-limited transformation pathways—a step beyond the observations reported in the paper.

paper_did: Prepared and characterized a six‐element high‐entropy alloy (TiZrHfMoCrCo) using levitation melting in argon, followed by sectioning and surface preparation.

Applied interventions by performing extended annealing at various temperatures (600 °C, 800 °C, 1000 °C for different durations) and high‐pressure torsion (HPT) (5 revolutions at 7 GPa, at room temperature) with/without subsequent annealing.
paper_reported: Identified a three‐phase microstructure in the as‐cast state: a body‐centered cubic (BCC / A2) phase along with two Laves phases (C14 and C15) with phase fractions of approximately 51%, 23%, and 26%, respectively.

Reported that annealing at 1000 °C causes the BCC phase to nearly vanish (with strong increase of the C15 phase and reduction of C14) while annealing at lower temperatures (600 °C and 800 °C) yields different Laves phase ratios and incomplete grain boundary wetting.

Showed that HPT significantly refines the grains, increases the BCC phase fraction (and eliminates C14), and that subsequent annealing at 1000 °C restores a phase composition similar to the as‐cast alloy annealed at the same temperature, along with distinct nanohardness and Young’s modulus differences between the phases.
paper_proposed: Proposed that varying combinations of heat treatment and HPT can be exploited to tailor the phase transformation pathways in the alloy, thereby expanding the range of accessible microstructures and mechanical properties.

Implied that phenomena such as grain boundary wetting and possible segregation effects (as well as defect accumulation) play key roles in driving phase transformations, suggesting further investigation into process–structure–property relationships.

Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by the competition between strong short‐range chemical ordering (predominantly Al–Co/Ni interactions) and the tendency of Cr and Fe to remain miscible in the BCC matrix. This competition drives a transformation near 600 °C wherein the formation of B2-ordered regions (rich in Co, Ni, and Al) leads to a compositional partitioning that leaves Cr/Fe-rich disordered domains.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature disordered BCC state (solutionized/annealed above the ordering temperature).
hypotheses.intervention: Conduct controlled cooling experiments with variable cooling rates through the critical temperature range (~600 °C).
hypotheses.conditions: Prepare samples homogenized at high temperature and then subject them to both slow cooling (allowing diffusion) and rapid quenching. Maintain identical ambient atmospheres to avoid oxidation effects.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The development of B2-ordered clusters (Co/Ni/Al rich) versus a remaining disordered Cr/Fe-rich matrix.
hypotheses.mechanism: At moderate cooling rates, the strong attractive interactions between Al and Co/Ni lower the free energy locally, triggering nucleation of B2 ordered regions. These regions promote a local depletion of Al (and concomitantly Co/Ni) from the matrix, thus indirectly driving Cr and Fe to remain or segregate in the disordered BCC phase. Fast quenching, in contrast, kinetically suppresses this ordering and limits compositional partitioning.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled samples will exhibit clear microstructural and diffraction evidence of two distinct regions: a B2-ordered phase enriched in Co, Ni, and Al and a disordered BCC phase enriched in Cr and Fe. The volume fraction of these phases may differ by an appreciable amount (order-of-magnitude change in peak intensities), while fast-quenched samples will retain a more homogeneous BCC structure.
hypotheses.baseline: A sample cooled at a conventional rate used in earlier studies, expected to produce only weakly developed ordering relative to the enhanced ordering under slow cooling.
hypotheses.boundary: The described mechanism is predominant in the temperature window around 600 °C; outside this range, either the disorder or complete ordering is stabilized.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the qualitative shift in phase fractions is expected, the exact quantitative differences in volume fraction and spatial scale of partitioning remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples, one slowly cooled and one rapidly quenched from the high-temperature BCC state. Characterize the microstructures using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and neutron or X-ray diffraction for B2 superstructure peaks.
measurements: Intensity and presence of B2 superlattice reflections in diffraction data
Spatial chemical segregation analysis via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) in TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both cooling protocols yield similar phase distributions without a significant enhancement of B2 peaks or chemical partitioning in the slow-cooled sample, the hypothesis—that cooling rate modulates phase stability via ordering kinetics—would be falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: Findings from the paper showing temperature-dependent development of short-range order and B2/BCC phase separation near 600 °C (e.g., PMC6207727::web::005, PMC6207727::web::014).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a direct controlled cooling test to link cooling rate with the competition between chemical ordering and phase separation—explicitly connecting short-range ordering terms to the eventual phase stability, which the paper did not experimentally vary.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is kinetically governed by the limited diffusion of Cr and Fe atoms. Enhancing their mobility via intermediate temperature annealing will allow the thermodynamic drive from Al–Co/Ni ordering to more fully manifest as compositional partitioning into two phases.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature homogeneous BCC state achieved by rapid cooling from above the ordering temperature.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a post-solidification annealing step at an intermediate temperature (~700 °C) for controlled periods (e.g., 1–10 hours).
hypotheses.conditions: After quenching from high temperature, anneal samples in a controlled inert atmosphere at 700 °C, where diffusion is sufficiently active yet below the melting point, then cool to room temperature at a fixed rate.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Growth of compositionally distinct domains: a B2-ordered region (rich in Al, Co, and Ni) and a Cr/Fe-enriched disordered BCC region.
hypotheses.mechanism: In the as-quenched state, kinetic limitations prevent full atomic reordering and phase separation. A dedicated annealing treatment at 700 °C enhances the diffusivity of Cr and Fe, permitting them to segregate from the regions forming a stable B2 order (driven by strong Al–Co/Ni bonds). This reduces the overall free energy by facilitating a complete partitioning based on the intrinsic enthalpy differences among the elements.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples undergoing extended annealing will display increased volume fractions and distinct microstructural domains evident via TEM and diffraction; DSC may show sharper peaks corresponding to phase transformations compared to unannealed samples.
hypotheses.baseline: An as-quenched sample from the high-temperature BCC state with minimal subsequent annealing, representing kinetically trapped, incomplete phase separation.
hypotheses.boundary: The effect is most pronounced in the intermediate temperature regime (600–700 °C) where diffusion is active but vibrational or complete melting effects are absent.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise kinetics (e.g., phase fraction changes and domain sizes) are not fully established, so only a qualitative enhancement in segregation is anticipated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the alloy: one subjected to an intermediate annealing step at 700 °C for varying durations and one without annealing. Characterize the evolution of microstructure using high-resolution TEM, elemental mapping (EDS), and DSC analysis to detect differences in phase separation.
measurements: Volume fraction and size of Cr/Fe-rich domains via TEM
DSC peak sharpening or shift indicative of phase transitions
Diffraction pattern differences in B2 superlattice intensities
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the extended annealing does not lead to a detectable increase in phase separation or alter the phase transformation signals compared to the as-quenched baseline, the hypothesis that kinetic diffusion limitations control phase stability is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s Monte Carlo simulations that reveal a sharp change in short-range order and Cr/Fe pair correlations near 600 °C (e.g., PMC6207727::web::014 and PMC6207727::web::017).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis explicitly tests the role of atomic mobility—by introducing a dedicated annealing step—to determine if diffusion limitations govern the degree of phase separation, a variable not directly controlled for in the original study.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is influenced by the coupling between chemical ordering and magnetic interactions in Cr and Fe. The onset of magnetic ordering at intermediate temperatures reinforces the chemical driving forces that segregate Cr/Fe from the non‐magnetic, strongly B2-ordering Co/Ni/Al regions.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in its high-temperature, disordered BCC state, prior to significant magnetic or chemical ordering.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply an external magnetic field during the heat treatment in the critical temperature range (~600 °C) to enhance magnetic ordering effects.
hypotheses.conditions: Conduct parallel heat treatments of samples at ~600 °C in an inert atmosphere: one set in a magnetic field of moderate strength (e.g., ~1 Tesla) and one set with no external field.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Enhanced magnetically driven alignment and segregation—the magnetic field is expected to promote ordering in the Cr/Fe component and strengthen the chemical partitioning between magnetically active and non-active regions.
hypotheses.mechanism: As the alloy cools through the intermediate temperature range, the magnetic moments on Cr and Fe begin to align, lowering the magnetic free energy. Under an applied field, this effect is amplified, driving Cr and Fe to energetically favor clustering into a magnetically ordered (and compositionally enriched) phase, while the Co/Ni/Al regions (which form a nonmagnetic B2 structure) are left behind. This coupling of magnetic ordering with chemical segregation stabilizes the two-phase microstructure.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples annealed under an external magnetic field will show a more pronounced separation between a magnetically ordered Cr/Fe-rich phase and a B2-ordered Co/Ni/Al phase, as evidenced by altered diffraction peak intensities and magnetic measurements (e.g., SQUID magnetometry) relative to the non-field-treated samples.
hypotheses.baseline: Samples heat treated at the same temperature and duration without an external magnetic field.
hypotheses.boundary: The effect is expected specifically in the temperature range where magnetic ordering of Cr/Fe is energetically viable (~600 °C). At higher temperatures, thermal agitation dominates; at much lower temperatures, diffusion may be too slow.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Due to limited direct literature on magnetic ordering in this specific high-entropy system, the magnitude and onset temperature of the magnetic contribution are somewhat uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Heat treat identical Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples at ~600 °C in two conditions: with and without an applied 1 Tesla magnetic field. Subsequently, use SQUID magnetometry to assess differences in magnetic ordering, and use diffraction (X-ray or neutron) and TEM to examine differences in phase distribution and superlattice ordering.
measurements: Magnetic hysteresis loops and onset of magnetic ordering (via SQUID)
Intensity changes in B2 superlattice peaks from diffraction data
Elemental segregation and domain structure via TEM and EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the application of a magnetic field does not result in any statistically significant enhancement of phase segregation or differences in the magnetic properties compared to controls, then the hypothesis that magnetic interactions substantially contribute to phase stability is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: Findings in the paper that establish strong chemical ordering in the B2 phase and composition-dependent segregation, combined with background principles where magnetic interactions (particularly in systems with Cr and Fe) can influence phase stability (as noted in superalloy strengthening discussions).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces an external magnetic field during processing as a means to probe the coupling of magnetic ordering with chemical segregation—an aspect not considered in the paper—to test if magnetism can be a decisive parameter in governing phase stability.

paper_did: Developed a Monte Carlo lattice simulation on a rigid BCC framework using nearest‐neighbor interaction parameters derived from first‐principles enthalpy matrices to study Al-containing HEAs.

Simulated the temperature‐dependent evolution in AlxCoCrFeNi alloys (with x ranging from 1 to 2), predicting a high-temperature disordered BCC phase that orders into a B2 structure—with Al favoring one sublattice and Co/Ni the other—and an ensuing phase separation near ~600 °C where Cr and Fe remain in a disordered matrix.

Conducted in situ experiments including neutron scattering (using an aerodynamic levitator), scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) with energy‐dispersive X‐ray spectroscopy (EDS), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to validate the simulation predictions.
Analyzed pair correlations (Pij) and long‐range order parameters (ηi) to correlate the evolution of chemical order with observed structural transformations.
paper_reported: The work reported that Al-containing HEAs undergo a two-step transformation: first from a high-temperature disordered BCC phase to a partially ordered B2 phase (with strong Al–Co/Ni interactions) and then a distinct separation near 600 °C where Cr and Fe preferentially remain in or segregate to a disordered BCC matrix.

The simulations quantitatively predicted trends in superlattice (B2) ordering and short-range chemical order (via Pij values) that match neutron diffraction and DSC data, including sensitivity to Al content (with higher Al content raising the B2 ordering temperature).

Experimental observations (e.g., changes in diffraction peak intensities, DSC peaks near 575–600 °C, and microstructural evolution in STEM images) corroborated the simulation’s prediction of a sharp, temperature-driven transformation associated with chemical ordering and phase separation.
paper_proposed: The paper proposed that the simulation approach—using first‐principles derived interaction parameters in a Monte Carlo framework—can be broadly applied to explore phase evolution in HEAs with limited experimental data.

It suggested that such a method could guide the design of ordered multiphase HEAs by mapping the temperature–composition space and identifying regions with potentially useful structural transformations.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by the kinetics of Al partitioning during cooling, where the diffusion‐mediated redistribution of Al from the supersaturated BCC matrix triggers local thermodynamic instability and nucleation of secondary phases. hypotheses.intervention: Apply two distinct cooling routes after solution treatment: a very high cooling rate (rapid quenching) versus a slower furnace cooling.
hypotheses.conditions: Keep all compositions and heat treatment durations identical except for the controlled cooling rate after the BCC state; use a quench media (e.g., water or oil) for rapid cooling and compare to furnace cooling.

hypotheses.mechanism: At high temperature the alloy is in a BCC state, but Al has a strong chemical driving force to partition because it destabilizes the BCC phase thermodynamically. During slow cooling, Al diffusion allows local enrichment and thus nucleation of secondary phases. In contrast, rapid quenching minimizes atomic mobility and suppresses this partitioning, maintaining the metastable BCC structure. This kinetic suppression is similar to the laser remelting effect discussed in PMC5043342::web::012 where rapid cooling inhibited phase precipitation.

hypotheses.uncertainty: Precise quantitative thresholds for cooling rates and the exact phase identity of the secondary phases depend on the detailed local thermodynamics of the alloy and require experimental mapping.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is primarily governed by the balance between the thermodynamic driving force for FCC transformation and the interfacial strain energy introduced by local lattice distortions (tetragonality) from atomic size mismatches. Reducing these lattice distortions by a controlled minor substitution should stabilize the high‐temperature BCC phase by reducing the nucleation rate of the FCC phase.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy in a high-temperature BCC state with existing local tetragonal lattice distortions due to atomic size differences and partial B2 ordering.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a small addition (e.g., approximately 1–2 at.%) of an isoelectronic element (such as Si) that has an atomic radius closer to the average of the constituent elements to reduce local lattice parameter variation and associated tetragonality.
hypotheses.conditions: Prepare two sets of alloys: the baseline Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 and the Si-modified alloy; employ identical melting, casting (arc melting), and quench conditions to achieve an initial high-temperature BCC state. Use EBSD and XRD at room temperature after quenching and during controlled thermal holds.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Interfacial coherence between BCC matrix and any emerging FCC/Widmanstätten plates, with reduced lattice distortions (lower tetragonality) leading to a less favorable transformation interface.
hypotheses.mechanism: The addition of Si is expected to minimize local lattice distortions by homogenizing the average atomic radii, thereby reducing the strain energy penalty at the BCC/FCC interface. This lowers the effective nucleation rate of the FCC phase (which originally nucleates via a dominant but slightly distorted Pitsch OR as identified in the paper) and thus kinetically stabilizes the BCC phase over a broader temperature range. The thermodynamic driving force remains, but the nucleation barrier is effectively increased.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The Si-modified alloy will exhibit a reduced volume fraction of FCC phase and a narrower distribution of orientation deviations (closer to the ideal Pitsch OR) compared to the baseline alloy. The transformation kinetics (for FCC phase formation) will be suppressed, indicating increased phase stability of the BCC state. The predicted change is of moderate magnitude; any significant decrease in FCC fraction (e.g., >10% decrease under identical conditions) supports the hypothesis.
hypotheses.baseline: The standard Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy showing a continuum of Pitsch-to-Kurdjumov–Sachs OR variants with evident lattice distortions and a significant FCC phase volume fraction after quenching.
hypotheses.boundary: Tested at similar high cooling rates (~100 K/s) and thermal regimes where the FCC phase nucleates via Pitsch OR with slight distortions. The hypothesis holds if the intervention affects phase stability without introducing new phases.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the trend is expected, the exact magnitude of FCC volume fraction change and orientation distribution refinement is uncertain due to multicomponent interactions.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: The extent of Al partitioning out of the BCC matrix.
hypotheses.mechanism: In a high-temperature BCC state, transformation to the lower-temperature equilibrium phase requires sufficient atomic diffusion, particularly of Al. Under slow cooling the longer residence time enables Al atoms to migrate, triggering local compositional fluctuations and nucleation of FCC or intermetallic phases. Rapid quenching, however, limits Al mobility, thus kinetically retaining the metastable BCC state. This mechanism couples the thermodynamic driving force for phase change (associated with Al’s influence on free energy) with diffusion kinetics.

hypotheses.boundary: The hypothesis applies when the cooling rates are sufficiently disparate to either enable or freeze out Al diffusion; at very low homologous temperatures (below ~1100 °C) additional transformation mechanisms might complicate the outcome.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact quantitative phase fractions depend on Al diffusion kinetics and the chosen cooling rate range.

Only when annealing conditions sufficiently increase atomic mobility do diffusion‐controlled processes enable detectable phase evolution.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Rapidly quenched samples will exhibit predominantly the high-temperature BCC phase. In contrast, samples annealed at higher temperatures and longer times will begin to show new phase features in XRD (e.g., emerging peaks corresponding to equilibrium phases), along with local compositional changes when analyzed by EPMA or atom probe tomography. The fraction of the transformed phase should increase with annealing temperature and time.
hypotheses.baseline: A sample that is directly quenched from the high-temperature state to prevent any significant atomic diffusion, thereby retaining the metastable BCC configuration.
hypotheses.boundary: The mechanism is operative only in temperature/time regimes where atomic mobility is the limiting factor. Below a critical annealing temperature or time threshold, no transformation is expected. Excessively high temperatures might lead to grain coarsening or other unwanted effects.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact activation energies for diffusion and the quantitative boundaries between kinetically trapped and transformed states are not fully established.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples annealed in regimes expected to overcome kinetic barriers do not show any significant onset of phase transformation relative to the rapidly quenched baseline, the hypothesis that sluggish diffusion governs phase stability is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: Existing knowledge that HEAs exhibit sluggish atomic diffusion, which is frequently invoked to explain their retention of metastable phases even when equilibrium thermodynamics might favor transformation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis explicitly correlates the kinetic limitations imposed by sluggish diffusion with the observed phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, providing a testable framework to quantify the temperature/time conditions needed to trigger phase transformations in these alloys.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is controlled by grain-boundary stabilization effects in its nanocrystalline structure. The high density of grain boundaries in the mechanically alloyed state provides a significant interfacial energy contribution that stabilizes the BCC phase against thermodynamic transformations to equilibrium phases.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 powders produced by mechanical alloying, exhibiting a high-temperature BCC phase with an ultrafine grain size.
hypotheses.intervention: Perform post-alloying treatments designed to induce controlled grain growth by annealing at a moderate temperature (e.g., 750 °C) for varying durations, compared with samples that are immediately consolidated to preserve the nanocrystalline state.
hypotheses.conditions: Anneal samples under inert atmosphere at temperatures high enough to promote grain coarsening (but below temperatures that would lead to complete phase transformation by diffusion) for different time spans (e.g., 30 minutes, 1 hour, and 2 hours); compare these to a rapidly consolidated baseline.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain size (and corresponding grain-boundary area) which contributes an additional free energy term that can stabilize the metastable BCC state.
hypotheses.mechanism: In nanocrystalline materials, the high density of grain boundaries contributes a sizable interfacial energy term. Owing to this, even if the bulk free energy favors a transition, the overall free energy of the nanostructured material may be minimized in the BCC configuration. As grain growth occurs during moderate annealing, the relative grain-boundary area decreases, diminishing this stabilization effect and allowing the thermodynamic driving force for transformation (e.g., to the equilibrium FCC or partially ordered phase) to dominate.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples that maintain a nanocrystalline grain structure (short or no annealing) will retain the metastable BCC phase, while samples that are annealed longer (and therefore exhibit larger grain sizes) will show an increased fraction of equilibrium phase features (such as the appearance of FCC peaks in XRD) and changes in mechanical properties (e.g., decreased hardness due to grain coarsening).
hypotheses.baseline: Mechanically alloyed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 immediately consolidated with minimal post-processing, preserving the ultrafine, high grain-boundary fraction BCC state.
hypotheses.boundary: The influence of grain-boundary stabilization is significant only in the nanocrystalline regime. If grains grow past a critical size where interfacial energy contributions are minor compared to bulk free energy differences, the mechanism may no longer operate.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of grain-boundary energy relative to bulk phase free energies in this specific HEA is not precisely known, and the critical grain-size threshold is uncertain.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis links the nanostructure of the mechanically alloyed Cr–Co–Fe–Ni–Al alloy directly to its phase stability, proposing that the grain-boundary energy term is a decisive factor controlling the retention of the high-temperature BCC phase under certain processing conditions.

paper_did: Synthesized three high entropy alloy (HEA) compositions – a Co‐free CrFeNiMo (HEA‐FREE), a Co‐containing Co0.5CrFeNiMo (HEA‐Co), and an Al‐substituted Al0.5CrFeNiMo (HEA‐Al) – from high‐purity elemental powders using mechanical alloying in a planetary ball mill.

Employed controlled processing parameters (ball‐to‐powder ratio, RPM, milling time, and use of 2 wt.% N‐heptane as a process control agent) and varied the milling conditions (e.g., lower RPM for Al‐containing alloy) to optimize alloying and homogenization.

Conducted extensive materials characterization including X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and elemental mapping for chemical homogeneity, and technological measurements (free flow, tap density, slope angle, packing ratio) to assess powder suitability for consolidation.
paper_reported: A high alloying degree was achieved after 30 hours of mechanical alloying; XRD analysis revealed the presence of two major crystalline phases (FCC and BCC) with peak broadening and intensity variations indicative of successful alloying.
Elemental mapping and EDS analyses confirmed a high degree of homogeneity and elemental distribution in all three HEAs, with no detectable oxygen contamination.

Technological characterizations indicated that the powders possess satisfactory flow and packing properties, rendering them suitable for further consolidation via techniques such as spark plasma sintering.
paper_proposed: Future work will focus on consolidating the mechanically alloyed powders into bulk materials (e.g., via spark plasma sintering) for use as electrodes in the electro-spark deposition process, ultimately aiming to produce corrosion-resistant coatings for aggressive environments.
